title: Restrictive vs Liberal Hemoglobin Transfusion After Cardiac Arrest
official: Restrictive vs Liberal Hemoglobin Transfusion After Cardiac Arrest
summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if a higher red blood cell count helps adults who stay on cardiac support and in a coma after cardiac arrest (when the heart stops). It will also learn if researchers can carry out this type of study on a larger scale. The main questions it aims to answer include:

* Do patients hearts and blood pressure recover sooner if they get blood transfusions to keep a higher red blood cell count?
* Can researchers enroll enough patients, follow the plan for blood transfusions, and reach participants for follow-up questions?
* How many participants survive, and how well do they function 6 months later?

Researchers will compare two ways of giving red blood cell transfusions. A common way to measure the red blood cells in the body is by looking at the hemoglobin level. There will be two strategies for transfusing blood.

* Higher level: Participants will get blood if their hemoglobin level goes below 9 g/dL. For these patients in the higher level group, the goal will be to keep the hemoglobin level at 9 or above.
* Lower level: Participants will get blood if their hemoglobin level goes below 7 g/dL. For these patients in the lower level group, the goal will be to keep the hemoglobin level at 7 or above.

It is not known which strategy is better. A higher level may help because red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body, and having more of them may help recovery after cardiac arrest. A higher level may be harmful because giving blood transfusions also comes with some risks. Doctors already use both approaches in usual care. Participants will be assigned by chance and have an equal chance of getting either transfusion strategy.

Because patients are in a coma, a family member or legal representative will need to give consent for them.

Participants will:

* Receive blood transfusions determined by the assigned strategy for 7 days
* Have no extra blood draws beyond usual care
* Have their health tracked in the hospital, including how long they need blood pressure medications
* Take part in a phone call at 180 days (6 months) about how they are doing in daily life; a family member or legal representative may answer for them
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Adult patients who survived for at least 6 hours after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)
* Post-arrest hemoglobin value of ≤9 g/dL at time of enrollment
* Comatose (not awake and following commands) after cardiac arrest and at time of enrollment
* Receiving vasopressors or inotropes at time of enrollment

Exclusion Criteria:

* Determined by the treating clinician to have an indication for a specific transfusion strategy
* Known to have a status of "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR) or "Do Not Intubate" (DNI) at time of enrollment
* More than 18 hours have passed since the time of ROSC
* Active hematologic disease, including hematologic malignancy and sickle cell anemia
* Patient expected to die or transition to comfort-focused care within 24 hours
* Patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) after ROSC
* Known to be a prisoner at time of enrollment
* Pregnant patients
